title: She Was Rejected From Luv Ranjan's Set at 17 — for Being Too Young. Now Sharvari Is in Talks to Headline His Next, Opposite Kartik Aaryan.
excerpt: The girl who once held the clap board on a Luv Ranjan film is now being courted to lead one. Sharvari's full-circle moment lands the same week her spy-universe debut, Alpha, hits theatres.
body:
Casting scoops come and go, but every so often one carries a story so neat you'd accuse a screenwriter of inventing it. This is one of those. **Sharvari** — the actress about to detonate the YRF Spy Universe with *Alpha* — is in talks to lead **Luv Ranjan's** next film, opposite **Kartik Aaryan**. And the reason it stings sweet is the part most people don't know: a decade ago, Ranjan looked at a seventeen-year-old Sharvari and told her she was too young for his movie.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=0d4nirTymmg</youtube>

The scoop, broken by Bollywood Hungama and quickly picked up across the trade, is still firmly in the 'talks' stage. But the contours are clear. Ranjan, the man behind *Pyaar Ka Punchnama* and *Sonu Ke Titu Ki Sweety* — arguably the sharpest Gen-Z romantic comedies of the last decade — wants Sharvari as his female lead.

> Sharvari has shown excitement, and is looking forward to collaborating with Luv Ranjan, the man behind some of the best Gen-Z films of the last 10 years. — Source, to Bollywood Hungama

Here's the timeline, because the studio choreography is half the fun. Ranjan is still writing. He intends to roll cameras by December 2026. He'll narrate the full script to Kartik first, then to Sharvari around August, and the paperwork follows once both have heard it end to end. Nothing is signed. But when a director of Ranjan's commercial pedigree is 'keen' and the actress is 'excited,' the gap between talk and ink tends to close fast.

Now the full circle. When Sharvari was seventeen, she auditioned for Ranjan's 2015 sequel and was turned down — too young, the makers decided, for an adult comedy. Most aspirants would have walked away bruised. She didn't. She joined the crew instead, working as a clap assistant director on his set, learning the machinery of a film from the floor up. She held the slate. She watched how the man built a scene. And now, eleven years later, she's the name he wants standing in front of his camera, not behind it. If you wrote that arc into a screenplay, an editor would call it too tidy.

It also lands at the precise moment Sharvari stops being an industry secret and becomes a headline. She earned genuine acclaim for **Imtiaz Ali's** *Main Vaapas Aaunga*, and she's about to go supernova: *Alpha*, the first female-led film in the YRF Spy Universe, hits theatres July 3, directed by Shiv Rawail and sharing the frame with **Alia Bhatt**, **Bobby Deol** and **Anil Kapoor**. Bhatt, in a birthday note ahead of the release, simply called her a 'star.' She's not wrong. Sharvari's *Alpha* teaser alone pulled the kind of numbers that make casting directors return calls within the hour.

And she isn't slowing down. After *Alpha*, she steps into **Sooraj Barjatya's** *Yeh Prem Mol Liya* opposite Ayushmann Khurrana, slated for late 2026. The Ranjan film, if it firms up, would be her third major confirmed project in a pipeline that suddenly reads like an A-lister's. The phrase the trade keeps using — 'the actor to look out for' — is starting to feel dated. She's already here.

For Kartik, the reunion is its own kind of homecoming. Ranjan is the director who made him a star with *Pyaar Ka Punchnama*; Kartik has said openly that his mentor 'gets the best out of him.' After a stretch of high-concept swings — *Captain India*, an Anurag Basu film, a Kabir Khan directorial — returning to the rom-com soil where he first grew is a canny move. Ranjan reportedly toyed with an action film, then abandoned it the moment a funnier idea took hold. He's doing what he does best. So, increasingly, is Kartik.

For the diaspora audience, a Kartik–Luv Ranjan rom-com is a near-guaranteed multiplex event from New Jersey to Southall to Brampton — their films travel, and they travel loud. Pair that bankable formula with Sharvari's rising heat and a backstory this poetic, and you have the makings of one of 2027's most-watched releases. First, though, the narration. Then the signatures. Then, if the gods of Bollywood scheduling are kind, the girl who once held the clap board gets to hear someone else call action for her.
